pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 74: Growing: tomato (2 m). Sweating: me.*

The second door was not a door. It was a gap in the hedge that looked like it had been cut with a dull knife. I pushed through the leaves, which smelled of sun and green sap, and stepped into heat that hit me like a physical wall. It was November, but here the air was thick and wet and buzzing. Cicadas droned in the branches, a sound so loud it felt like it was coming from inside my own ears.

Rows of tomato plants stretched out before me, staked to wooden poles that stood in perfect, rigid lines. There was a lemon tree in the center, its branches heavy with bright yellow fruit that looked hard enough to dent. The vegetable bed was enormous, easily the size of the school hall, and every single inch of it was covered in deep green leaves.

I stood there. My mouth was open. I forgot to count the seconds. I forgot to check if anything was growing too fast. For nearly an hour, I just walked. I touched the leaves. I smelled the dirt. I did not rush. The garden did not ask me to. It just was.
pages.image: Sana, in a denim jacket, stands dwarfed by towering green tomato plants and a lemon tree in a vibrant, sun-drenched garden; her expression is one of wide-eyed wonder as she reaches out to touch a leaf.

pages.text:
The Summer Room had a thirst that made math look cruel. My can held four liters, but one hundred plants needed four liters each, twice a day. That meant eighty trips, which is a lot of running for a girl who usually walks.

On the first day, I sprinted. I filled the can, dumped the water, and ran back, feeling like the main character in a movie where nobody asks you to stop. By day five, my legs ached and my back felt like I had been filled with wet cement from a construction site. By day ten, I was grumpy, and my smile had the quality of a forced customer service script.

Theo arrived with a backpack and a look of supreme confidence, having been watching me from the fence with the stillness of a cat waiting for a treat. He held up two fingers. We split the work. We made it a game: if we finished before the sun hit its high point, we won.

Yusuf was not invited to the game. He was appointed Chief Puddle. He had his own small watering can, a red plastic one that leaked like a broken faucet. He watered his shoes first. Then he watered the air. He declared the puddle on the path "perfect" and moved on to the next plant, spraying half the water directly onto my socks.
pages.image: Theo and Sana stand side by side in a row of tomato plants, holding watering cans, looking determined; Yusuf, in a red shirt, is in the foreground watering his own sneakers with a small, leaking red can.

pages.text:
Mr. Osei was at the loading bay again, his blue overalls bright against the grey concrete. He did not look at me, but his hands were clasped behind his back, fingers interlaced so tightly that his knuckles turned white.

I watched him from my window, holding the heavy can. I wanted to go down and ask him why he stood there, or if he could see the tomatoes and the lemon tree, the life I was feeding every morning. He stood for an hour. Then he turned and walked away without a sound.

I filled the can again. My arms shook, and I thought about the notice on the door. One year. That is three hundred and sixty-five days of watering. That is one thousand and forty-five trips, which is more steps than I have taken since we moved here. I looked at the fence. I looked at the can. The number felt very large, like a math problem in a book I would rather not open.
pages.image: Sana peers from a fourth-floor window holding a watering can, looking down at Mr. Osei who stands by a chain-link fence with his back to her, gazing at a patch of green; the scene is lit by late afternoon sun.

pages.text:
I took the stairs because the lift was out of order again, which meant ninety-two steps instead of forty seconds of standing still. Mrs. Ilves was on the landing, knitting a scarf that had already grown longer than I was tall, her needles clicking with a steady, rhythmic sound that cut through the quiet of the stairwell.

"You are tired," she said.

"I am doing the math," I replied.

She stopped knitting and looked at me, her eyes sharp and kind. "People who have lost someone often cannot go near the thing they loved," she said. "It hurts too much. It isn't lack of caring. It is an excess of it."

She went back to her knitting. I stood there, holding the can. The water inside sloshed gently against the metal, a small, heavy churning that felt less like a liquid and more like a debt I had signed up for without reading the fine print. I carried it to the bottom of the stairs and walked out to the garden, trying to keep the surface level, trying not to spill a single drop.
pages.image: Mrs. Ilves sits on a concrete stair landing, knitting a long scarf, while Sana stands nearby holding a watering can; the lighting is soft and dim, highlighting the texture of the wool and Sana's serious expression.

pages.text:
The tomato was the size of a marble, red and smooth and warm from the sun that seemed to exist only inside these walls. I looked at it, then at Gherkin, who was asleep on a patch of moss near the humming bench.

"Can I pick it?" I asked the plant.

It said nothing. The leaves did not move, and the cicadas hummed their low, droning song. I reached out, my fingers closing around the stem, and it snapped with a clean, soft click. I held it in my palm. It was perfect. I bit into it, and the juice was sweet and thick, tasting like the middle of July, a memory of heat that shouldn't be possible in November.

I broke it in half and held one piece out to Yusuf, who was watching from behind the hedge. I held the other out to Theo, who was pretending to be asleep. I ate the stem, which was bitter, but it was mine. This was what the waiting was for.
pages.image: Sana holds a single, small red tomato in her hand, offering half of it to Yusuf and Theo who are peeking out from behind green foliage; her face is illuminated by a warm, golden light that contrasts with the grey concrete in the background.
